sections.heading: 4. Price the information advantage against the canonical operating economics
paragraphs: Keep the scorecard fixed while evaluating tools. Conservative annual gross equipment resale proceeds are $250,000 at a 10% net margin, producing $25,000 owner net profit with two full-time staff and four contractors. Base proceeds are $1,025,000 at 16.0%, producing $164,000 with the same four-person pod. Scaled proceeds are $1,800,000 at 22%, producing $396,000 with three full-time staff and five contractors. The corresponding total expense envelopes are $225,000, $861,000, and $1,404,000; acquisition and refurbishment are already inside those envelopes. Do not subtract acquisition twice or treat equipment purchase principal as separate customer transaction volume. The stated startup capital range is $20,000 to $95,000, monthly operating expenditure range is $4,000 to $18,000, and first-deal horizon is three to nine months. Those ranges are planning constraints, not additional amounts to append mechanically to each scenario. A proposed subscription, inspection package, or contractor retainer must either fit the modeled expense envelope through an identified allocation or appear in a separately labeled sensitivity. Information tooling does not automatically improve the canonical margin. It earns its budget by preventing measurable losses, reducing paid work, or enabling documented equipment sales without exceeding the team's delivery capacity.

Underwrite individual assets with a cash bridge that keeps contribution distinct from annual owner profit. For an illustrative $40,000 resale, $24,000 acquisition, $4,000 refurbishment, $2,000 freight, and $1,000 selling and warranty provision leave $9,000 before shared overhead and other annual expenses. That $9,000 is transaction contribution, not the Base case's 16.0% owner margin applied to a single device. If inspection identifies another $3,000 repair, contribution falls to $6,000 unless acquisition price or another cost changes. Use this bridge to value research: a $300 specialist review is attractive when it answers a material question before an irreversible purchase, but its value is not established by counting database fields. For a separate tooling sensitivity, an incremental $250 monthly subscription costs $3,000 annually. At unchanged Base revenue and all other costs, owner profit would become $161,000, so preserving the canonical $164,000 requires an equal documented offset or a different operating change. Do not bury that subscription inside an asserted automation benefit. Track prevented purchases using the original bid packet and the discovered defect, but distinguish such avoided exposure from realized cash savings. Unspent speculative capital is useful, yet it is not additional booked equipment revenue.

Run a weekly operating review around inventory age, evidence completeness, contractor turnaround, and cash committed to unresolved assets. The sourcing operator owns qualified opportunities and buyer confirmations; the operations operator owns blocked records, release packets, and refresh failures. Measure contractor workload in inspection hours, sanitization jobs, transport events, and specialist reviews rather than assuming four contractors equal four full-time employees. Limit simultaneous acquisitions to the number the pod can inspect, store, document, and sell within its cash capacity. For diagnostic replacement sourcing, review manufacturer support and installed-option risks before negotiating collection. For surgical surplus recovery, review lot-level accessory completeness and decontamination evidence before assigning a blended bid. For veterinary/aesthetic matching, review intended use, buyer requirements, and device-specific obligations before promising compatibility. Use age-based alerts to trigger a documented price review, parts disposition assessment, or buyer campaign; never erase a failed asset from the denominator. Compare actual gross resale proceeds and total expenses against the chosen canonical case every month. Move to the Scaled staffing assumption only when additional throughput supports three full-time staff and five contractors within the $1,404,000 expense envelope. The operational advantage is a shorter, better-supported decision cycle, not a larger database whose inspection backlog ties up the same scarce capital.

chapters.subtitle: FDA Servicing Boundaries, UCC Title Protection, HIPAA Media Controls, State Device Licenses, and Buyer-Ready Contract Scripts
chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #14, Medical Equipment Resale, holds Rank #20 with a Money-to-Manpower Score of 85/100. This chapter maps three operator plays: documented diagnostic resale, service-backed surgical resale, and specialty veterinary/aesthetic resale with intended-use separation. Contracts must connect clean title, device identity, service scope, patient-data removal, and buyer acceptance before inventory becomes cash. The canonical annual owner-profit cases are $25,000 Conservative, $164,000 Base, and $396,000 Scaled, on gross equipment resale proceeds rather than brokerage fees. A two-employee, four-contractor pod can execute the first two cases by outsourcing specialized evidence gathering without outsourcing accountability. The scaled case expands to three employees and five contractors. Protect margin by rejecting unsupported devices before purchase, not by arguing over disclaimers after delivery.

sections.heading: 1. Classify the device and the work before acquiring inventory
paragraphs: Build the legal file around the actual device and transaction, not the phrase refurbished equipment. Candidate #14 has three mapped operator plays in this chapter: documented diagnostic resale, service-backed surgical resale, and specialty veterinary/aesthetic resale with intended-use separation. For each prospective purchase, record the manufacturer, model, serial number, available UDI, intended use, accessories, software revision, labeling, and ownership chain. Search FDA recall records and relevant clearance or approval records using the exact model family; a registration entry does not establish clearance, approval, or current condition. The commercial lead owns supplier representations, while the operations lead owns the evidence folder and exception log. A contracted biomedical technician verifies identity and condition against manufacturer documentation. Another contractor handles specialist work only within documented competence. For diagnostic systems, distinguish ordinary ultrasound equipment from radiation-producing systems with additional installation duties. For surgical equipment, identify reusable components and processing instructions before promising a complete usable package. For specialty equipment, separate veterinary labeling from human aesthetic claims. Changing the advertised patient population or treatment purpose can change the regulatory analysis even when nobody opens the enclosure. Stop purchase negotiations when identity cannot be reconciled across the chassis, service records, invoice, and installed software.

The central FDA boundary is between restoring a finished device to its established specifications and performing work that significantly changes performance, safety specifications, or intended use. FDA describes the latter as remanufacturing; calling the invoice servicing does not control the outcome. Use 21 CFR 820.3 and FDA's servicing and remanufacturing guidance to document the actual activities, including replacement components, software changes, energy output, alarm behavior, and treatment claims. The Quality Management System Regulation became effective February 2, 2026; determine the applicable manufacturer obligations under current Part 820 rather than recycling an obsolete quality-system checklist. Ordinary domestic distribution may qualify for the registration exemption in 21 CFR 807.65, but importing, relabeling, repackaging, or remanufacturing requires a separate role analysis. Registration, listing, premarket authorization, reporting, and quality-system duties are distinct questions. Require the biomed contractor to describe both the work performed and the specifications used for release. A successful power-on test does not prove alarm accuracy, electrical safety, image quality, or performance under load. When a replacement board or software image lacks a traceable specification, keep the unit outside saleable inventory until the responsible specialist resolves the change and records the resulting regulatory position.

Apply a second screen for condition, claims, and post-sale events. The Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act prohibits specified dealings in adulterated or misbranded devices under 21 U.S.C. 331; a used-device label does not erase those restrictions. Prescription-device labeling under 21 CFR 801.109 also makes purchaser qualification and intended use operational questions, not just marketing preferences. Keep manufacturer instructions and warnings with the delivered configuration, and identify missing manuals before quoting. Avoid promising FDA approval merely because a device has a 510(k) clearance or an establishment has registered. Veterinary-only devices generally do not follow the human-device premarket authorization pathway, yet adulteration and misbranding concerns remain; human aesthetic claims cannot borrow that distinction. Establish a complaint channel tied to serial numbers, with immediate escalation for injury allegations, unexpected treatment output, contamination, and failed safety functions. Determine whether Part 803 medical-device reporting or Part 806 correction and removal duties apply to the business's actual role. Do not assume every reseller has identical reporting obligations. Contractually require prompt cooperation, record preservation, and customer-location tracking. The operations lead should be able to identify every affected buyer without searching personal inboxes or relying on a departing contractor's memory.

Retain a clean model-specific listing template so sales staff cannot accidentally carry human treatment claims into veterinary inventory.

sections.heading: 2. Resolve destination licensing, patient data, and contamination
paragraphs: Create a location-and-activity worksheet before soliciting binding purchase orders across state lines. List the seller's premises, storage site, service location, buyer destination, installer, device type, and intended clinical use. State requirements can attach to manufacturing, prescription-device distribution, home medical equipment services, radiation equipment, or professional operation; one business license does not answer all six questions. California Health and Safety Code section 111615 addresses device manufacturing licensing, while Florida Statutes section 499.01 establishes permits for covered activities, including prescription-device wholesale distribution. Check definitions, exemptions, and the responsible agency's current instructions against the actual transaction rather than assuming every used-equipment seller needs the same permit. Diagnostic X-ray transactions require additional attention to state radiation registration, qualified installation, shielding, and inspection requirements. Federal assembler reporting under 21 CFR 1020.30 may also apply to diagnostic X-ray assembly activities. Aesthetic laser ownership does not establish permission to practice medicine or operate the device in every state. Veterinary purchasers likewise need an intended-use and operator analysis appropriate to their practice. Assign counsel a bounded question with the worksheet attached, request a written answer, and record the renewal or recheck date alongside the inventory record.

Treat stored patient information as a purchase-condition problem before transport begins. Ultrasound consoles, imaging workstations, endoscopy processors, and connected service laptops may retain identifiers, images, worklists, credentials, or remote-access settings. HIPAA does not automatically cover every reseller; determine whether the seller is a covered entity and whether the reseller or sanitization contractor will act as a business associate. Where that relationship exists, use the required agreement under 45 CFR 164.504(e) before permitted access, and address subcontractors. The device and media controls in 45 CFR 164.310(d) distinguish disposal from media reuse. Prefer seller-side sanitization verified before pickup, with an exception process for equipment that cannot be cleared without specialist intervention. Specify authorized methods using current NIST SP 800-88 guidance and manufacturer constraints; factory reset alone is not evidence that all storage has been cleared. Record media identifiers, method, verification results, technician, date, and custody transfers without copying patient content into the certificate. Where storage removal disables licensed software or calibration, price authorized restoration before accepting the unit. Prohibit diagnostic uploads containing patient records to ordinary sales tools, and restrict quarantine access to the personnel needed to resolve the exception.

Decontamination evidence must travel separately from the electrical test report because the two answer different questions. Ask the seller which surfaces, lumens, probes, accessories, and packaging were processed, using which instructions and by whom. A wipe-down receipt cannot support a sterile claim, and a passing leakage-current test cannot establish infection-control readiness. For reusable surgical components, preserve manufacturer processing instructions and define whether final processing occurs before shipment or at the buyer's facility. Do not let ordinary resale expand silently into reprocessing single-use devices, which can introduce manufacturer obligations. Where employees face occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials, apply 29 CFR 1910.1030 through exposure controls, training, protective measures, and appropriate handling procedures. Establish physically separated received, quarantined, serviced, and released inventory areas. The two employees remain the commercial and operations leads; the four contractor slots cover biomed service, data sanitization, logistics, and specialist legal or regulatory support. These slots are planned capacity, not permission to use unqualified generalists for every procedure. Use external certificates as evidence while retaining an internal release decision. If either sanitization or contamination status remains unresolved, stop shipment and reserve the resulting storage and remediation cost against that unit's expected contribution.

sections.heading: 3. Write contracts that preserve title, acceptance, and unit economics
paragraphs: Use paired acquisition and resale agreements with serial-specific schedules, not a generic invoice followed by contradictory email promises. The acquisition schedule should identify included probes, carts, cables, software rights, manuals, service records, and excluded consumables. Require the seller to represent ownership, authority to sell, and disclosed liens, leases, security interests, and recall history. UCC section 2-312 addresses title warranties; state enactments and negotiated language determine the actual transaction terms. Search relevant UCC records using the seller's correct legal identity and obtain specific lien releases where necessary. Under UCC section 9-315, a security interest can continue in collateral after disposition unless an authorization or other applicable rule changes that result. Do not assume possession or a paid invoice cleans title. Identify who can reject the unit, which evidence triggers rejection, and who pays return freight, storage, and hazardous-condition handling. For the diagnostic play, attach image-quality and accessory tests. For the surgical play, attach function, processing, and component criteria. For specialty resale, attach the exact intended-use statement and software configuration. The commercial lead owns negotiation; the operations lead confirms the promised deliverables exist before either agreement is signed.

Define the payment trigger and acceptance process independently. A deposit reserves identified inventory under stated refund conditions; it does not prove delivery or authorize immediate revenue recognition. The sale agreement should specify shipment terms, risk of loss, insurance, installation responsibilities, an objective inspection window, the test protocol, and remedies for documented nonconformity. If acceptance depends on installation, state what happens when the buyer delays site readiness and distinguish that delay from a failed device. For a separate sourcing engagement, identify the fee trigger precisely, such as a completed qualifying purchase, and avoid charging an unstated fee alongside the resale price. These canonical scenarios describe principal equipment resale, not agency commissions. Gross proceeds of $250,000 at 10% yield $25,000 annual owner profit; $1,025,000 at 16.0% yields $164,000; $1,800,000 at 22% yields $396,000. Acquisition and refurbishment are included in those margins. As an illustrative unit check, a $41,000 sale supporting the Base margin permits $34,440 of fully allocated costs and leaves $6,560 profit. Twenty-five such sales reproduce the Base totals exactly. Include freight, contractor work, warranty provision, storage, and allocated overhead in that cost envelope rather than subtracting only the purchase price and calling the balance owner profit.

Draft warranty and liability language around evidence the business can actually support. Under UCC sections 2-313 and 2-316, factual sales promises and warranty exclusions interact; an inspection report or listing can create obligations that a broad condition label does not erase. Define warranty duration, covered components, response process, exclusions, and responsibility for travel and freight. A negotiated liability cap might reference the affected unit's purchase price, but specify treatment of bodily injury, fraud, title defects, indemnities, and data incidents rather than assuming every claim is capped. UCC section 2-719 and state law can limit remedy restrictions. Use a narrow anti-circumvention clause only for identified introductions, with a defined duration, preexisting-relationship exception, and proportionate remedy reviewed for enforceability. Select governing law, venue or arbitration, notice methods, and an escalation timetable. For IP and data ownership, separate physical hardware title from OEM software licenses, service manuals, calibration tools, and patient records. Patient information is not saleable inventory merely because it remains on a drive. Require authorized license transfer where needed and preserve the buyer's access to agreed service records. Finally, make insurance requirements match actual device categories and territories; a certificate alone does not establish that product liability or installation work is covered.

sections.heading: 4. Use precise outreach scripts and retain the evidence behind every claim
paragraphs: Build outreach around equipment identity and documented capability, not dramatic revenue claims for the buyer's practice. For commercial email, CAN-SPAM requirements under 15 U.S.C. 7704 include truthful routing information, nondeceptive subject lines, required advertising identification where applicable, a valid physical postal address, and a working opt-out mechanism; business-to-business messages are not categorically exempt. Honor opt-outs within the statutory period and retain suppression records when contractors manage campaigns. For telephone and text outreach, analyze 47 U.S.C. 227, current FCC rules, number type, dialing technology, prerecorded content, applicable permission, and state restrictions before activating automation. A published clinic number is not universal permission for every channel or technology. The default small-pod workflow is individually researched business email and manually placed calls through an approved contact list. Use this seller discovery script verbatim: 'We purchase documented used medical equipment for resale. Are you authorized to sell this unit, and can you provide the model, serial number, service history, lien or lease status, and processing record? Please do not send patient images or records. We can discuss value after reviewing identity, condition, software transferability, and pickup requirements.' Record the answers without converting unverified seller statements into advertising claims.

For diagnostic buyers, use this discovery script: 'Which procedures and installation environment must this system support? We will quote the exact model, software revision, probes, documented service work, and acceptance tests. Please identify your authorized purchasing contact and technical reviewer. We will confirm available evidence before making performance or delivery commitments.' For the surgical play, ask separately about reusable accessories, processing capability, site power, and the party responsible for final preparation before use. For specialty veterinary/aesthetic resale, use this boundary script: 'Is the intended use veterinary or human clinical treatment, and in which state will the equipment operate? We will evaluate the device's labeling and configuration for that use rather than assume the same unit can serve both markets.' If asked whether a unit is FDA approved, answer from the record: 'We distinguish clearance, approval, registration, and device condition. We will provide the applicable authorization reference and our inspection scope; we will not describe registration as approval.' These questions identify real purchase dependencies while keeping the seller outside clinical recommendations. Never promise reimbursement eligibility, treatment outcomes, or professional permission from the equipment sale alone. Route clinical selection questions to the buyer's qualified personnel and document the configuration they request.

Close with an evidence-first quotation rather than an unsupported urgency pitch. Use this script: 'Our quotation covers the identified unit and listed accessories, documented service scope, shipping terms, and agreed acceptance tests. Software transfer, installation, processing responsibilities, and any unresolved dependencies are stated separately. Please confirm your technical reviewer and destination requirements before we schedule shipment.' When a prospect declines, reply: 'Understood. We will stop promotional outreach through this channel and record your preference.' Do not require a purchase, login, or explanatory call to process an email opt-out. The commercial lead maintains approved scripts, quote versions, and suppression records; the operations lead approves serial-specific evidence and release status. Inventory tracking and service-history indexing are the two automation levers: use them to assemble quote attachments and flag missing documents, not to invent inspection results. Review exceptions weekly, including title gaps, stale licenses, unresolved recalls, storage exposure, and unpriced warranty work. The Conservative and Base cases retain two employees plus four contractors; the Scaled case requires three employees plus five contractors. Do not claim the higher case preserves the four-person pod. With $20,000–$95,000 startup capital, $4,000–$18,000 monthly operating expense, and three to nine months to first deal, disciplined rejection protects runway as much as disciplined selling generates receipts.

chapters.question_prompt: How does a 1 FT + 3 C (4 people) medical equipment resale team automate 70%+ of repetitive research, qualification, fulfillment, and traffic/deal acquisition while keeping human-in-the-loop QA?

chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #14, Medical Equipment Resale, ranks #20 with a 85/100 Money-to-Manpower Score because automation accelerates evidence handling, not physical refurbishment. This chapter maps three operating plays: diagnostic fleet refresh, surgical equipment redeployment, and veterinary/aesthetic specialty resale. A 1 FT + 3 C pod connects serial-level inventory, service-history indexing, buyer qualification, and distribution through durable Python jobs and evidence-constrained language models. Biomed personnel retain release authority; commercial staff retain pricing and claims authority. The canonical annual owner profits remain $25,000 Conservative, $164,000 Base, and $396,000 Scaled, with the last case requiring 1 FT + 3 C. Measure 70%+ automation against a fixed repetitive-work denominator, including exception handling, rather than counting generated listings as completed deals.

sections.heading: 1. Build one serial ledger and divide the four-person pod by decision authority
paragraphs: Organize Candidate #14 around three explicitly mapped operating plays: diagnostic fleet refresh for imaging and diagnostic instruments, surgical equipment redeployment for documented systems and accessories, and veterinary/aesthetic specialty resale for devices with verified intended use and service support. These are operating lanes, not separate revenue forecasts. Give the first full-time operator purchasing, pricing, cash allocation, and buyer commitments; give the second inventory control, evidence quality, workflow maintenance, and dispatch coordination. Assign four contractors to biomedical evaluation, specialist repair, decontamination and preparation, and freight and installation coordination, subject to actual qualifications. Contractor availability must appear as booked capacity rather than assumed continuous coverage. Across all three plays, the shared automation backbone performs intake normalization, document indexing, buyer matching, and status propagation. It never determines electrical safety or invents missing maintenance. Reserve two daily exception windows so purchasing questions do not interrupt every bench task. Each unresolved item receives an owner, evidence request, and expiration time. When specialist capacity is full, purchasing slows before unfinished inventory consumes cash. This division preserves the canonical 1 FT + 3 C constraint while making the actual bottleneck visible: qualified release hours, not the number of descriptions a model can draft.

Create a Python service around a serial-level asset ledger, initially using sqlite3 transactions and an append-only event table on a single managed host. Assign an internal asset UUID because manufacturer serial formats can collide across brands. Store manufacturer, model, serial, configuration, accessory manifest, acquisition cost, location, custody, commercial reservation, and technical status separately. A technical state machine moves from received to quarantined, evaluated, repaired when necessary, tested, and released; commercial states track available, reserved, sold, and returned. A released asset can still be unavailable because another buyer holds its reservation. Use UNIQUE constraints for external event identifiers and atomic conditional updates for reservation changes. Link service documents through immutable object identifiers, hashlib SHA-256 digests, document dates, and controlled storage locations. Preserve revisions instead of replacing old evidence. A nightly reconciliation compares physical location scans, reservations, marketplace listings, and the accounting inventory balance. Begin with a CSV exception report that a person can understand before adding dashboards. Test duplicate serials, partial kits, missing probes, and returns with changed accessories. An elegant record that cannot distinguish the machine from its separately priced transducer will create expensive fulfillment errors long before it creates useful automation. Photograph labels during intake and reconcile them against the ledger before any listing leaves draft.

Treat supplier forms, marketplace notifications, and freight callbacks as untrusted events entering the same durable inbox. Verify provider signatures using hmac.compare_digest where the provider supports shared-secret signing, enforce timestamp tolerance, and record the event before acknowledging receipt. Fetch authoritative order details through authenticated APIs when callbacks contain only references. A worker validates the schema, checks asset identity, performs the permitted transition, and writes an outbound task within the same database transaction. This transactional outbox prevents a successful reservation from losing its listing-removal request during a crash. Workers retry transient failures with bounded exponential delays and jitter; permanent validation failures move to an exception queue. Never retry a payment, shipment purchase, or buyer message blindly after a timeout. First query the provider using the original idempotency key or order reference. An inventory heartbeat detects stale integrations and suspends affected channel availability until reconciliation. Keep a printable released-stock list and a controlled manual reservation log for outages, then merge those entries before restarting publication. Log actor, previous state, new state, evidence identifiers, and correlation ID without copying patient information into application logs. Recovery must restore the physical-commercial truth, not merely restart a process that was already publishing the wrong stock.

sections.heading: 2. Index service histories without delegating safety, patient-data handling, or device claims
paragraphs: Service-history indexing begins with a restricted document landing area, not a public chat interface. Classify incoming files by asset, document type, date, source, and potential patient content. An operator separates service records from clinical exports, DICOM studies, screenshots, and embedded storage images before any external model submission. Where the relationship creates business associate duties, execute the required agreement and configure safeguards before handling electronic protected health information for the covered entity. HIPAA applicability depends on the parties and activity; purchasing used equipment alone does not resolve that analysis. Apply 45 CFR 164.310(d) media controls where applicable and select sanitization procedures appropriate to the actual storage technology. A factory reset is evidence of a reset, not proof that every storage component was sanitized. Inventory removable disks, service partitions, printer storage, and cached network credentials. Record the method, verification result, technician, asset identifier, and disposition of failed media. If sanitization would damage validated configuration or licensed software, stop and obtain an authorized service path. Keep clinical material out of the resale knowledge base; a service index should answer what was tested and repaired, not reveal who was examined. Restrict access by role and retain only the records necessary for the documented transaction and applicable obligations.

For cleared records, combine OCR with a constrained extraction request that returns document date, observed serial, procedure, measured results, parts replaced, software revision, and supporting page references. Python's json module can parse the response, but application validators must enforce required fields, length limits, allowed units, and exact asset matches. Treat every document instruction as source text, never as permission to change the extraction policy or contact another service. Use SQLite full-text search when available, with a keyword fallback, before buying a separate vector database. Retrieve the smallest relevant packet and require each generated claim to cite an existing document and page. Missing preventive maintenance becomes a request for evidence, not a fabricated interval or a reassuring adjective. Confidence scores prioritize review; they do not establish accuracy. A model can draft a service chronology, identify contradictory dates, and flag a serial mismatch, while a qualified reviewer resolves those conflicts. Build a test corpus containing rotated scans, handwritten corrections, mixed-device invoices, and superseded reports. Measure field-level precision, unsupported claims, serial attribution errors, and review minutes. A shorter summary that omits an uncertain assertion is operationally superior to a polished narrative that attaches another machine's calibration certificate.

Separate ordinary servicing from changes that could make the business a remanufacturer. FDA's servicing and remanufacturing guidance focuses on whether activities significantly change performance, safety specifications, or intended use; a cosmetic label such as refurbished does not settle the classification. Route changed energy output, altered software functions, substituted critical components, and modified intended-use claims to device-specific assessment before work or marketing proceeds. Where manufacturer requirements attach, evaluate registration and listing under 21 U.S.C. 360 and 21 CFR Part 807, applicable premarket obligations, and the Quality Management System Regulation under 21 CFR Part 820. Do not automatically assign those obligations to every domestic reseller, and do not assume a reseller exemption covers importing or manufacturing activities. Identify state licensing and radiation-control requirements for the equipment and destination. Surgical systems need accessory and sterilization compatibility evidence; diagnostic systems need configuration and performance evidence; veterinary/aesthetic transactions need especially careful intended-use and buyer-use checks. Veterinary-only status does not make a device exempt from every applicable control. The publication workflow should block unsupported safety, certification, clearance, and outcome claims. Release requires a signed technical packet and a separately reviewed commercial description, both linked to the exact configuration offered rather than merely the model family.

callout.body: Automation can assemble the packet, but named reviewers must close these four checks for the actual serial and offered configuration.

sections.heading: 3. Turn released inventory into programmatic, referral, and outbound distribution loops
paragraphs: Build programmatic distribution from released inventory rather than generating thousands of speculative product pages. Each asset page should expose verified configuration, included accessories, documented condition, supported service region, shipping constraints, and an appropriately redacted evidence summary. Publish availability from the reservation ledger and remove purchase actions immediately when stock becomes unavailable. Separate durable model-family guides from serial-specific offers so sold stock does not leave a trail of misleading availability. Google Search Console can identify useful queries, but search impressions are not qualified demand. Measure inquiries that identify a buyer, use case, destination, budget range, and purchasing timeframe. Diagnostic fleet refresh pages answer probe compatibility and installation questions; surgical pages explain complete-system and accessory boundaries; veterinary/aesthetic pages distinguish documented intended use from buyer assumptions. Use actual photographs with licensed rights and redact hospital identifiers. A Python publishing job renders approved fields into templates, validates outbound links, and queues previews for commercial review. Only previously approved factual fields may update automatically afterward. Material configuration or performance changes require fresh review. Maintain a page revision identifier on every inquiry so the sales operator can reconstruct precisely what the buyer saw, including the offered accessories and stated delivery conditions at the time of contact.

Create an evidence-sharing loop that helps a buyer complete internal evaluation. After qualification, issue an expiring link to a redacted technical packet containing the actual serial, configuration, test summary, accessory checklist, and delivery requirements. Let the buyer invite their biomedical engineer or procurement colleague without exposing another customer's records or unrestricted service files. Track packet requests and subsequent questions at the account level rather than treating every recipient as a new lead. Successful installations can produce permissioned case studies about operational facts, such as configuration delivered and installation coordination, without patient outcomes or unsupported clinical claims. Service contractors can refer facilities planning replacements, while satisfied buyers can request alerts for matching inventory. Keep referral compensation transparent and review arrangements that intersect federally reimbursed business before implementation, including potential 42 U.S.C. 1320a-7b(b) exposure. Avoid paying clinicians simply for steering reimbursable business. The flywheel is specific: better evidence shortens technical diligence, completed transactions produce permissioned references, references attract better sellers and buyers, and better acquisitions improve the next evidence packet. Measure each link separately. A widely forwarded packet that produces no suitable inquiries has generated distribution activity, not a proven acquisition advantage or permission to increase inventory commitments.

Outbound begins with a small, documented account universe, not scraped personal contact lists. Segment facilities by supported equipment family, geography, service coverage, and plausible replacement timing. Use public organizational information and authorized CRM records to draft relevant messages without asserting that a facility owns a particular machine unless that fact is verified. For commercial email, implement accurate sender information, nondeceptive subjects, a valid postal address, and functioning opt-out handling under 15 U.S.C. 7704. Synchronize suppression records before every send and honor applicable opt-out deadlines. Do not silently expand the workflow into automated calling or texting; those channels require separate analysis of applicable rules. A human approves the initial segment, offer, and message template. Automation may then match released assets, prepare individualized drafts, schedule permitted sends, and route replies. Buyer qualification extracts requested configuration, intended use, location, installation needs, and timeline, but humans resolve suitability and unusual payment or export arrangements. Stop sequences immediately on a reply, opt-out, reservation conflict, or stale availability signal. Attribute deals using account and asset identifiers, deduplicate referrals against outbound records, and report acquisition cost per completed sale. More email cannot compensate for an unavailable device or a buyer whose installation requirements the pod cannot support.

callout.title: Make the evidence packet do the selling
callout.body: Experienced equipment traders reduce buyer uncertainty before increasing traffic. These tactics strengthen all three operating plays.
items: Photograph the serial plate, software version screen, connectors, and included accessories during one controlled intake session; reusing verified images prevents repeated warehouse interruptions.
Index service histories by serial plus component identifier, not only model name; probes, handpieces, and modules often carry the evidence that determines whether a system is saleable.
Record doorway dimensions, lift requirements, receiving hours, and installation responsibility before quoting freight for large diagnostic or surgical systems.
Keep sold model-family pages useful with factual buying guides and opt-in availability alerts, while clearly removing the sold serial from active purchase and reservation paths.

sections.heading: 4. Prove automation economics, rehearse recovery, and scale only the supported workload
paragraphs: Define the 70% target before instrumenting the workflow. Use repetitive task episodes such as intake normalization, service-document indexing, qualification-field extraction, shipment-status routing, and approved availability updates. Freeze the task taxonomy and baseline handling times for the measurement period; do not split easy tasks into smaller units after seeing results. An illustrative monthly cohort contains 1,000 episodes, of which 740 complete correctly without human intervention and 260 require exception work. That yields 74% touchless completion, but it does not automatically yield 74% labor savings. If baseline repetitive handling averages six minutes per episode, the original load is 6,000 minutes. At five minutes per exception, plus 200 minutes of sampled review and 200 minutes of maintenance, the remaining repetitive-work burden is 1,700 minutes: a 71.7% reduction. Validate those times through observation rather than adopting them as operating facts. Technical testing, physical preparation, commercial release, and consequential buyer decisions remain outside the repetitive-task denominator and still require staff capacity. Report their hours beside the automation percentage so leadership cannot mistake narrower administrative savings for whole-business automation. If rework or monitoring increases, include it immediately. A single erroneous configuration propagated to six channels is one source defect with six cleanup obligations, not six successful automated episodes.

Price automated runs using explicit assumptions and reconcile them to the scorecard without claiming that software creates additional margin automatically. For an illustrative indexed-document run, assume 8,000 input tokens at $2 per million and 1,000 output tokens at $8 per million, producing $0.024 of model usage. Add $0.010 for OCR and $0.006 for allocated queue, storage, and compute: $0.040 per run. These are planning assumptions, not vendor quotations. At 1,000 runs, direct usage is $40. If a costed review sample covers 10% of runs for two minutes each at $45 per hour, it adds $150, or $0.190 per run including that review. This narrow sample matches the 200 review minutes above but excludes exception labor, maintenance, physical work, and fixed business software. The canonical Conservative case remains $250,000 revenue less $225,000 total costs, yielding $25,000 owner profit. Base remains $1,025,000 less $861,000, yielding $164,000; Scaled remains $1,800,000 less $1,404,000, yielding $396,000. These are gross equipment resale proceeds, not commission revenue or customer equipment value handled for others. Acquisition and refurbishment stay inside the cost envelope. Allocate payroll, contractor utilization, freight, returns, insurance, storage, and automation within those totals rather than adding imagined savings to the stated owner profits.

Run a monthly recovery exercise on a copy of operational data with patient material excluded. Replay duplicate callbacks, interrupt an outbound listing update, expire an API credential, submit an unreadable service scan, and reserve the same asset concurrently from two channels. Expected behavior is controlled quarantine, one valid reservation, preserved evidence, and a visible owner for each unresolved exception. Restore a backup into an isolated environment and compare asset counts, reservation balances, document hashes, and open shipment references before declaring recovery successful. During model outages, revert to deterministic field extraction and manual indexing; during marketplace outages, stop affected publication and maintain the source ledger. During carrier outages, prepare documents manually but confirm whether a shipment already exists before purchasing another label. Review aging stock weekly by model support, parts availability, carrying cost, and realistic exit value. Automation should accelerate markdown or parts-recovery decisions when evidence supports them, not conceal unsellable inventory behind fresh traffic. The Scaled case explicitly expands to 1 FT + 3 C; assign added capacity to the measured bottleneck rather than claiming the four-person pod produces that case unchanged. Buy additional inventory only when released-stock throughput, specialist availability, cash conversion, and exception burden support it. The distribution flywheel must remain subordinate to device safety and cash discipline.

chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #14, Medical Equipment Resale, holds Rank #20 with a 85/100 Money-to-Manpower Score: capital discipline and technical accountability matter more than headcount compression. This chapter maps three operator plays: diagnostic equipment refurbishment, surgical equipment resale, and veterinary/aesthetic equipment remarketing. Run them through one serial-level operating system, initially staffed by 1 FT + 3 C and expanded only to 1 FT + 3 C when throughput supports it. Canonical annual owner net profits are $25,000 Conservative, $164,000 Base, and $396,000 Scaled. Protect those economics with accepted-work contractor payments, weekly exception reviews, counterparty concentration limits, and clean accrual cohorts. Build transferable records and delegated relationships before discussing an exit multiple; otherwise, the buyer is purchasing the owner's job.

sections.heading: 1. Assign eight possible seats without building eight departments
paragraphs: Build one shared pod around three explicitly mapped plays: diagnostic equipment refurbishment, surgical equipment resale, and veterinary/aesthetic equipment remarketing. These are operating lanes for Candidate #14, not separate businesses with duplicated managers. In the four-person configuration, the owner occupies the first full-time seat as commercial lead and capital allocator; the second full-time employee owns inventory operations, document control, and collections coordination. Four contractors provide biomed testing, rigging and freight, technical sales support, and bookkeeping with data-hygiene coordination. The coordinator does not personally certify unfamiliar device sanitization; qualified personnel must perform and document the actual work. Assign a named person, backup method, deliverable, and spending limit to each seat. Contractors are fractional capacity, not four hidden full-time salaries. At scale, add an employed technical operations lead and a fifth contractor covering specialist field service. That produces exactly three employees and five contractors, including the owner, rather than quietly introducing another management layer. The technical lead controls release evidence while the owner retains capital allocation. No person may buy equipment, accept its technical condition, authorize their own disputed invoice, and release the same payment without an independent documented review.

Each play needs a distinct acceptance packet inside the same inventory system. Diagnostic units require model-specific functional checks, accessory inventories, applicable calibration evidence, and software-transfer verification; an ultrasound console without a transferable option can be worth materially less than its listing suggests. Surgical equipment requires instrument compatibility, insulation or electrical testing where applicable, and a documented decontamination handoff. Veterinary and aesthetic devices require intended-use classification, consumable availability, service access, and verification that performance claims match the actual configuration. Veterinary devices do not automatically inherit every human-device regulatory obligation, and aesthetic branding does not remove medical-device obligations. Use Odoo Inventory or an equivalently controlled serial ledger, with service histories indexed by serial number and revision. Store signed reports in a restricted repository, not personal messaging threads. For each incoming machine, identify the legal seller, title evidence, installed software rights, accessories, recall status, and location before committing refurbishment money. A hospital asset tag establishes identity, not necessarily transferable ownership. Confirm financing releases and relevant UCC searches when warranted. This shared evidence architecture lets six people handle three plays without relearning the equipment's history at every handoff.

Set contractor compensation around bounded deliverables instead of vague availability. Offer the biomed contractor an agreed diagnostic fee, a separate authorized repair budget, and payment for a complete test packet, regardless of whether the machine passes. Paying only for passing devices creates the wrong incentive. Freight contractors receive route-specific quotes with declared value, loading responsibility, packaging scope, and claims deadlines. Technical sales support earns a fee on collected, positive-contribution transactions after the contractual return period, with written treatment of later refunds. The bookkeeping contractor receives a monthly close retainer plus a separately priced historical cleanup scope. Illustrative service targets are intake acknowledgment within one business day, initial biomed findings within three business days after receipt, and complete shipping evidence within one day of dispatch. Parts shortages pause completion clocks only through recorded exceptions. Do not use contractor labels to bypass employee classification; evaluate actual control, independence, applicable federal standards, and state tests. At $250,000 revenue, the entire annual expense envelope is only $225,000, including acquisition and refurbishment. If two genuinely staffed employee seats and required contractor coverage cannot fit, that scenario fails local underwriting; unpaid labor is not a repair.

sections.heading: 2. Run the weekly scorecard from serial-level exceptions
paragraphs: Run a forty-five-minute weekly operating review from a frozen Monday export, not an improvised slide deck. The operations coordinator publishes every owned serial, cash invested, days in each state, next action, accountable seat, and expected cash conversion date. Keep distinct states for received, quarantined, under diagnosis, awaiting parts, technically released, listed, contracted, shipped, accepted, and collected. The owner reviews cash commitments before discussing sales volume. Track rolling thirteen-week gross proceeds, collected cash, acquisition commitments, landed inventory cost, repair spending, contribution by device cohort, and warranty exposure. For contractors, show completed jobs and denominators: six accepted reports from seven submitted is more informative than a green quality badge. Separate first-pass documentation acceptance from actual device pass rate; difficult equipment can legitimately fail functional testing while the contractor performs excellent work. Establish initial internal targets of at least 95% complete packets and 90% on-time milestones, then recalibrate using observed job complexity. Never reward faster release by allowing unresolved safety defects. Review every disputed invoice, overdue receivable, and machine with no credible next action. Close the meeting with a named owner and dated correction for each exception.

Adopt a concentration policy capped at 25% for any single customer group's trailing-twelve-month recognized revenue and any single supplier group's trailing-twelve-month acquisition spending. Aggregate entities under common control; splitting purchase orders does not diversify exposure. Apply the same ceiling to individual customer groups' outstanding receivables and supplier groups' open advances, with a separate dollar limit where small denominators would distort decisions. Model post-transaction exposure before accepting the next purchase or sale. Early operations can exceed percentage limits mechanically because one first transaction represents all activity; disclose the breach and suspend additional unsecured exposure rather than presenting startup concentration as resolved. Use diversified prospecting, deposits, staged purchases, and alternate approved suppliers to reduce exposure. Contractor continuity needs its own metric: identify which released inventory depends on a single technician, software account, or service-key holder. Backup qualification is not an extra full-time seat, but paid backup work must still enter the expense ledger. Track aging alongside concentration because five unrelated buyers do not help if all owe overdue balances. Receivables follow-up belongs to operations; commercial concessions require the owner's authorization and a recorded effect on transaction contribution.

Translate exceptions into economically bounded decisions. At thirty days without diagnosis, stop buying the affected model until the technical bottleneck is understood. At sixty days awaiting unavailable parts, obtain a second sourcing assessment and compare continued repair with parts recovery or liquidation. At ninety days without qualified buyer activity, refresh comparable sale evidence, listing accuracy, and expected recoverable value; age alone does not determine the accounting write-down. These are internal escalation thresholds, not promises of market liquidity. For diagnostic equipment, track probe failures and unavailable software options separately. For surgical equipment, track incomplete accessory sets and failed safety checks. For veterinary/aesthetic equipment, track consumable lockouts and unsupported installation requirements. Inventory tracking and service-history indexing are Candidate #14's two automation levers: automate reminders and evidence links, not technical conclusions. A Zapier notification can flag an expired calibration certificate, but cannot establish that a device is safe. Contractor disputes should reference the agreed test protocol, missing evidence, and correction deadline. Pay undisputed accepted work on schedule. Repeated missed milestones trigger reduced assignments or replacement after continuity planning, while unsafe work triggers immediate shipment suspension for the affected units.

sections.heading: 3. Close accrual books that survive serial-by-serial diligence
paragraphs: Maintain clean accrual accounts with an individual cost record for every machine and a consistent policy for shared costs. Candidate #14 recognizes gross equipment resale proceeds when acting as principal, not the hospital's original purchase price, downstream clinical billings, or financing principal. A brokerage arrangement in which the business acts only as agent requires a separate principal-versus-agent assessment and may recognize only the fee; do not mix that activity into the canonical resale scenarios without reconciliation. Capitalize equipment purchase cost and qualifying directly attributable inbound freight and refurbishment costs under the adopted accounting policy. Expense selling, administrative, and other period costs consistently. Recognize revenue under the contract's transfer-of-control terms, considering substantive acceptance conditions; a deposit or unsigned shipment receipt is not automatically earned revenue. Keep refundable deposits in liabilities. Release the matched inventory cost to cost of goods sold when the related sale is recognized. Accrue incurred but unbilled repair work and estimate applicable warranty obligations. Reconcile the serial subledger, general ledger, bank accounts, payment processors, and physical inventory each month. A spreadsheet can support this process, but uncontrolled overwrites and untraceable manual plugs cannot.

Reconcile every dashboard to the three canonical cases without turning an attractive unit spread into owner profit. Conservative revenue of $250,000 at 10% produces $25,000 annual owner net profit and $225,000 total scenario expenses. Base revenue of $1,025,000 at 16.0% produces $164,000 owner net profit and $861,000 expenses. Scaled revenue of $1,800,000 at 22% produces $396,000 owner net profit and $1,404,000 expenses. Acquisition and refurbishment sit inside those expense envelopes, alongside other costs included by the scorecard. Do not subtract acquisition twice or add inventory purchases directly to accrual expenses before sale. As an illustrative Base bridge, forty-one completed sales averaging $25,000 reconcile exactly to $1,025,000 gross proceeds; the actual mix can differ. The Base expense allowance averages $21,000 per completed sale, leaving $4,000 owner profit per sale after all allocated scenario expenses. These averages are budgeting checks, not device-level pricing rules. Track diagnostic, surgical, and veterinary/aesthetic cohorts separately because warranty experience, turnaround, and obsolete parts differ. Show purchases, recognized revenue, ending inventory, returns, repair overruns, and owner profit in separate columns so cash absorbed by unsold stock remains visible.

A transferable close package also connects technical records to legal and commercial rights. Classify each modification before authorizing work: FDA's servicing-versus-remanufacturing framework turns on the activity's effect on safety, performance specifications, or intended use, not the contractor's preferred label. Applicable manufacturer obligations, including the Quality Management System Regulation in 21 CFR Part 820, require a device-specific assessment; ordinary resale alone does not automatically create them. Document decontamination methods, materials compatibility, and exposure controls where employee occupational exposure invokes 29 CFR 1910.1030. Equipment containing electronic protected health information requires a defined custody and sanitization path. HIPAA applicability depends on the parties and functions; a business-associate relationship requires the applicable contract and safeguards, while covered entities retain their own duties. Use device-compatible sanitization procedures, verification results, and exception quarantine rather than a generic factory-reset claim. Never copy patient records into sale listings or buyer diligence folders. Check state device, radiation, and facility-related requirements for the actual equipment and activities. Record test instrument calibration, technician qualifications, software entitlement, and warranty scope beside the serial ledger. A profitable sale with missing rights or unresolved contamination can become a post-close liability.

sections.heading: 4. Build transferable earnings before negotiating an exit multiple
paragraphs: Transferability starts with rights and relationships, not a valuation spreadsheet. Obtain signed contractor agreements covering confidentiality, access termination, return of records, and ownership of commissioned reports, listing photography, original procedures, and inventory automation. Under 17 U.S.C. section 204(a), a copyright ownership transfer generally needs a signed writing from the owner or authorized agent; paying an invoice does not by itself transfer copyright. Do not rely casually on work-made-for-hire language for independent contractors. Schedule preexisting contractor materials and specify a durable license where assignment is unavailable. Neither arrangement creates rights to copy OEM manuals or transfer restricted diagnostic software. Keep vendor portals, domain registrations, CRM exports, telephone numbers, and repository administration under company-controlled accounts with individual access. Review customer, supplier, landlord, software, and service agreements for assignment and change-of-control conditions. For each material relationship, establish a second company contact and retain communication history. Demonstrate that operations can complete a purchase, technical release, shipment, collection, and warranty response while the owner is absent. A thirty-day delegation exercise exposes missing authority more reliably than a polished procedure binder. Resolve failures before asking a buyer to pay for institutional capability.

Value the business using a defined earnings measure and a clearly stated transaction perimeter. For planning sensitivity only, consider 2.0–3.0 times normalized seller's discretionary earnings for an owner-operated equipment trader and 3.0–4.5 times normalized EBITDA for a genuinely manager-run operation with transferable records and diversified counterparties. These are illustrative negotiating ranges, not observed comparable transactions or promised market pricing. Obtain current broker and buyer evidence before setting an asking price. The canonical $25,000, $164,000, and $396,000 owner net profits are neither automatically SDE nor automatically EBITDA. Bridge interest, taxes, depreciation, owner compensation, personal expenses, unusual costs, and necessary replacement labor explicitly. A buyer cannot add back the owner's work and simultaneously assume that work disappears. Only if diligence establishes Base normalized SDE at exactly $164,000 does the illustrative 2.0–3.0 range imply $328,000–$492,000 of operating business value on the stated earnings basis. Only if Scaled normalized EBITDA independently equals $396,000 does 3.0–4.5 imply $1,188,000–$1,782,000. Neither calculation changes the canonical scorecard. At Conservative earnings, replacement labor may absorb the economic return, making recoverable asset value more relevant than an attractive headline multiple.

Negotiate inventory and working capital explicitly before comparing offers. An asset sale may price equipment inventory separately, while another transaction includes a normalized working-capital amount in enterprise value. Define the treatment of saleable inventory, obsolete units, deposits, receivables, warranty obligations, debt, and cash; never add the same inventory value twice. Use a seasonal monthly working-capital history rather than one unusually lean closing balance. In a cash-free, debt-free structure with an agreed working-capital target, equity proceeds generally reconcile from enterprise value through debt, cash, working-capital adjustments, and transaction costs. Earnouts, escrows, seller notes, and retained liabilities can make a higher headline offer less valuable than a lower cash offer. If retaining the business, use the same discipline: distribute cash only after funding inventory commitments, expected repairs, taxes, and a documented liquidity reserve. The stated $20,000–$95,000 startup capital and $4,000–$18,000 monthly operating expense ranges are planning context, not incremental deductions from already reconciled owner profit. Promote the eight-person pod only when incremental capacity pays for its real costs. A durable cash cow is a repeatable cash-conversion system, not a warehouse whose paper margin depends on another large speculative purchase.

chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #14, Medical Equipment Resale, ranks #20 with a Money-to-Manpower Score of 85/100. This sprint maps three concrete operator plays: diagnostic ultrasound resale, nonimplantable surgical equipment resale, and veterinary ultrasound resale. The first month purchases evidence before inventory: documented buyer demand, transferable ownership, device-specific biomed testing, decontamination records, and verified data removal. A 1 FT + 3 C pod works within a $15,000 monthly operating cash ceiling and a $15,000 initial inventory exposure limit. Day 30/60/90 decisions distinguish repairable commercial gaps from stop-work safety failures. Canonical annual owner net profits remain $25,000 Conservative, $164,000 Base, and $396,000 Scaled. Because first deals normally require 2–7 months, early Scale decisions authorize controlled learning, not speculative purchasing.

sections.heading: 1. Days 1–7: Narrow Three Plays and Protect the First $75,000
paragraphs: Treat the first week as an evidence sprint rather than an auction shopping trip. Candidate #14 has a 85/100 score because capital exposure and hands-on verification constrain leverage; a clean spreadsheet cannot neutralize an obsolete probe or disputed title. For this chapter, map exactly three launch plays: diagnostic ultrasound resale to outpatient practices, nonimplantable surgical equipment resale to surgery centers, and veterinary ultrasound resale to established clinics. These are execution lanes, not additional scorecard candidates. Start with one supported model family per lane and select one winner before buying. Aesthetic lasers remain a research-only adjacent category until the team documents model-specific service access, calibration capability, buyer restrictions, and insurance coverage. Assign FT1 to sourcing, buyer discovery, pricing, and collections; assign FT2 to custody, documentation, inventory control, and release coordination. The four contractors cover biomedical inspection, specialist repair and decontamination, equipment logistics, and device regulatory plus data-security review. Select contractors whose actual credentials cover those scopes; do not assume one generalist can certify every device. Their booked hours must fit the cash plan. No person substitutes sales urgency for independent technical acceptance, and neither founder releases their own undocumented repair.

Use the lower end of the stated $20,000–$95,000 startup range to make scarcity explicit. Illustratively allocate $45,000 to three months of operating cash, $15,000 to initial inventory exposure, and $15,000 to an untouched exception reserve. The monthly operating ceiling is $15,000, within the canonical $4,000–$18,000 range: $6,500 for combined founder cash pay, $3,500 for the contractor pool, $2,000 for storage and insurance, and $3,000 for software, professional review, sourcing travel, and general shipping. These are planning allocations, not market salary claims; record deferred founder compensation separately and include economically required labor in pricing. Device acquisition, committed repairs, and attributable freight together consume the $15,000 inventory envelope. Allocate contractor work between overhead and unit cost without counting it twice. Stop new discretionary commitments when actual plus committed monthly operating cash reaches $12,000; the remaining $3,000 completes existing obligations. Never bridge a shortfall with refundable buyer deposits. The initial $75,000 supports only this bounded test, not the full nine-month sales horizon. Before Day 60, secure additional runway or reduce future commitments enough to preserve orderly closure and customer obligations.

Build the evidence ledger on Day 1 in Airtable or an equivalent access-controlled inventory database, with QuickBooks Online holding accounting rather than technical truth. Give every candidate a permanent asset identifier and fields for model, serial, accessories, seller ownership, lien inquiry, service history, software entitlement, decontamination, data status, biomed results, location, and disposition. Index documents by asset identifier in a restricted document repository; never upload patient records merely to make service histories searchable. By Day 7, complete twelve discovery interviews, four in each play, and obtain at least six written sourcing leads. An interview counts only when an authorized buyer states their application, budget range, purchase horizon, required accessories, and acceptance criteria. A supplier lead counts only with model, serial evidence, asking price, and authority to sell. Use FDA classification resources and current device-specific requirements to separate ordinary resale from activities that could constitute manufacturing or remanufacturing. Check applicable state requirements for the seller location, storage location, and intended destination. Record the basis for each decision and the responsible reviewer. The weekly deliverable is a ranked model-family shortlist with explicit exclusions, not a warehouse full of discounted equipment.

callout.body: Experienced resellers price the missing pieces before they negotiate the visible machine.
items: Photograph probe model numbers, connector pins, cable strain relief, and serial labels; a console price without usable probes is an incomplete acquisition quote.
Ask the OEM or authorized service channel about software entitlement transfer before purchase; a working demonstration does not establish transferable feature rights.
Request the hospital surplus release and any lender payoff evidence together; the department disposing of equipment may not control encumbered title.

sections.heading: 2. Days 8–14: Turn Supplier Claims into Releasable Asset Evidence
paragraphs: Week two converts a promising listing into an inspectable asset without assuming ownership prematurely. Request a serial-specific document packet before traveling: proof of authority, maintenance records, configuration screenshots with patient information excluded, accessory inventory, incident disclosures, and storage conditions. Search FDA recalls by manufacturer and model, then establish whether the serial falls within affected production and whether the corrective action was completed. The absence of a search result is not a service certificate. For financed equipment, obtain appropriate lien searches and a release or authorized disposition where required; UCC section 9-315 explains why a security interest can continue after disposition. Have the biomedical contractor write model-specific acceptance tests before inspecting: ultrasound image uniformity, probe integrity, ports, battery condition, and supported software are examples, not a universal test standard. Surgical tables require load, articulation, braking, accessory fit, and applicable electrical checks under the manufacturer's procedures. Veterinary use does not excuse unreliable hardware or contaminated accessories. By Day 10, require three complete inspection dossiers and two independent service estimates. A seller who blocks serial verification or controlled inspection leaves the acquisition queue immediately, regardless of the advertised discount.

Design custody so the team can prove what happened between pickup and buyer acceptance. The logistics contractor photographs the serial, cosmetic condition, accessories, packaging, and handoff at each transfer. Mark incoming equipment quarantined until decontamination and technical checks are complete. Follow manufacturer-compatible cleaning methods and document chemicals, contact times, operator identity, and limitations; surface cleaning does not establish that an invasive accessory is sterile or reusable. Exclude single-use accessories from any informal reuse plan. For data-bearing equipment, ask the seller to remove patient information before transfer and obtain evidence, then independently verify accessible storage and configured network destinations. Factory reset alone may leave DICOM studies, removable media, credentials, or service logs. Use manufacturer-supported erasure or media replacement methods that preserve safe device function and transferable software rights. Where the reseller performs services involving protected health information for a covered entity, assess business associate status and establish the required agreement before access. Apply 45 CFR 164.310(d) disposal and reuse safeguards where applicable. An accidental patient-data discovery triggers isolation and the agreed incident process, not screenshots in the sales chat. Release records contain verification results, not copies of the patient material removed.

Keep the servicing boundary visible in every work order. Restoring a device to its original specifications differs from changing intended use or significantly altering safety or performance; actual activities determine whether remanufacturing obligations arise. Do not represent an ordinary resale business as automatically subject to every manufacturer requirement, and do not assume the word refurbished creates an exemption. The reviewer determines the relevant obligations under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and implementing rules, including 21 CFR Part 820 when the activity makes the business a covered manufacturer. Prescription-device distribution and labeling under 21 CFR 801.109 require a separate device-specific review. Check intended application, buyer eligibility, labeling, and destination before issuing a binding offer. On Day 12, run a mock release using one complete dossier; every missing record becomes a named corrective task. On Day 13, compare the three plays using verified demand, supported service access, all-in cash exposure, and probable time to acceptance. On Day 14, select one pilot asset or record a deliberate no-purchase decision. Both outcomes are valid if they protect capital and document why the evidence did or did not support a transaction.

callout.title: Four Independent Checks Before Money or Equipment Moves
callout.body: Commercial interest never substitutes for the evidence needed to own, handle, or release a device.
items: Ownership check: match seller authority, serial evidence, and applicable lien release before paying an acquisition balance.
Technical check: require signed model-specific biomed results and completed corrective work before removing quarantine status.
Data and contamination check: verify compatible decontamination and storage sanitization, with every exception resolved before outbound release.
Commercial check: obtain a qualified buyer profile, complete landed-cost worksheet, and cash forecast that preserves the $15,000 exception reserve.

sections.heading: 3. Days 15–21: Sell a Documented Configuration and Test the Unit Economics
paragraphs: Week three tests whether a buyer will pay for the exact configuration the pod can deliver, rather than for a generic model name. Prepare a serial-specific offer with dated condition photographs, included probes or accessories, supported software features, test results, delivery responsibilities, installation boundaries, and acceptance criteria. Use eBay Business and Industrial, DOTmed, direct outreach, and local service partners as discovery channels, while following each channel's applicable listing rules. Asking prices indicate competition, not realized value; preserve closed-sale evidence or actual written buyer responses separately. Send at least six offers by Day 21, covering all three plays, but describe unowned equipment accurately as subject to availability and inspection. Do not publish patient-bearing screen images or claim OEM certification without substantiation. A qualified offer identifies the buyer, application, configuration, total delivered price, expected decision date, and unresolved conditions. Require a named clinical or technical acceptance contact, not merely an enthusiastic intermediary. For diagnostic and veterinary ultrasound, demonstrate the required application using suitable test methods rather than repurposed patient studies. For surgical equipment, verify receiving-site dimensions, utilities, and accessory compatibility before treating the quote as actionable demand.

Use an explicitly illustrative pilot worksheet to expose margin leakage. A $20,000 equipment sale might require $10,000 acquisition, $1,500 refurbishment, $600 inbound freight, $400 decontamination and data work, $500 testing, $800 outbound freight, $400 transaction costs, and a $600 warranty provision. Those $14,800 attributable costs leave $5,200 contribution, or 26%, before general overhead and owner economics. This is a screening example, not a fourth canonical scenario. Its pre-sale inventory exposure is $13,000 through testing; a conservative cash forecast also reserves outbound and transaction payments. Count testing contractor charges once, even when the same contractor also consumes the monthly retainer allocation. A 10% realized-price reduction to $18,000 leaves only $3,200 contribution, about 17.8%, if attributable costs remain unchanged. That sensitivity explains why the launch requires at least 25% projected contribution and a positive downside contribution before purchase. The canonical annual cases remain $250,000 revenue at 10% net margin for $25,000 owner profit, $1,025,000 at 16.0% for $164,000, and $1,800,000 at 22% for $396,000. Gross equipment resale proceeds are revenue; taxes collected, refundable deposits, and hypothetical buyer treatment revenue are not.

Make the commercial experiment reversible until the asset passes its release checks. Prefer seller-held inspection windows or clearly documented conditional purchase arrangements over speculative stockpiling. If using consignment, specify title, custody, insurance, selling authority, service spending, and return rights; report commission activity separately rather than presenting it as gross resale revenue in the canonical cases. The core launch model here remains purchasing and reselling owned equipment. FT1 logs every objection and next decision date; FT2 updates actual and committed cost daily. Contractors execute bounded work orders with change limits, not open-ended restoration projects. Establish a maximum $1,000 unplanned repair allowance within the existing $15,000 exposure ceiling; anything larger requires re-underwriting or withdrawal before further discretionary work. A buyer deposit remains a liability until earned under the contract and applicable accounting treatment. Record acceptance conditions and refund exposure before accepting it. By Day 21, the pod should possess six issued offers, two written buyer responses with concrete objections, one complete pilot cost sheet, and a documented reason to buy or wait. A disciplined wait is superior to a purchase that creates inventory merely to make the sprint appear productive.
