sections.heading: 4. Days 22–30 and Reviews at 60/90: Kill the Hazard, Fix the Constraint, Scale the Evidence
paragraphs: The final nine days convert scattered activity into a decision packet the four-person pod can defend. On Days 22–24, reconcile supplier claims against inspection findings, complete a delivery dry run, and have an independent reviewer sample the pilot dossier. On Days 25–27, conduct buyer follow-ups, update signed quotation assumptions, and build a thirteen-week cash forecast that distinguishes operating payments, inventory commitments, restricted deposits, and the exception reserve. On Days 28–30, score each play, reconcile all commitments, and issue a written Kill, Fix, or Scale decision. The metrics count distinct counterparties and serial-specific candidates; repeated calls and revised quotes do not manufacture progress. Define an active opportunity as a named buyer with application fit, stated budget, an identified decision contact, and a dated next step within thirty days. Define a release-ready asset as one with every mandatory technical, ownership, data, and distribution condition satisfied. Zero unresolved critical exceptions is mandatory in every window. Any suspected unsafe device, compromised patient information, or defective ownership evidence immediately stops movement of the affected asset while the responsible specialist determines containment and remediation. Commercial scores never offset those failures.

Apply the decision matrix in order: hard-stop conditions first, all Scale conditions second, and Fix otherwise. A Kill decision normally closes an asset or play, not automatically the entire company; inability to fund existing obligations or preserve the exception reserve stops new company-wide commitments. At Day 30, Scale means permission to run one controlled pilot under the original limits after eighteen qualified interviews, six eligible sourcing leads, six issued offers, three active opportunities, and one release-ready candidate. At Day 60, require twenty-four interviews, ten offers, five active opportunities, and two release-ready candidates to expand sourcing work, not inventory exposure. At Day 90, purchasing expansion requires one completed, accepted, collected resale with at least 25% actual contribution, three further active opportunities, and replacement working capital. Without that sale, a valid funded pipeline remains Fix, consistent with the canonical 3–9 month time to first deal. An asset aged over sixty days triggers a written liquidation quote and carrying-cost review; ninety days prohibits another purchase in that model family until the stock is sold or a funded exit is documented. Calendar pressure is never a reason to falsify readiness.

Give Fix a short clock and a specific experiment: ten business days, one accountable founder, and at most $2,000 of already available operating budget, with no increase to the monthly ceiling. Examples include five new buyer interviews after weak demand, a second service estimate after excessive repair pricing, or a manufacturer-supported erasure procedure after incomplete storage verification. Failed safety remediation kills the affected asset; repeated commercial weakness kills the lane under the matrix thresholds. At Day 90, a qualified Scale decision can permit a second concurrent asset only with separately funded working capital, the protected $15,000 reserve, and a forecast covering six months of planned operating outflows. Keep the launch pod at 1 FT + 3 C until actual workload warrants change; the canonical Scaled case uses 1 FT + 3 C and cannot be claimed by simply multiplying pilot contribution. Reconcile gross resale proceeds, acquisition and refurbishment costs, overhead, warranty expense, and economically required labor before comparing annual net margins. Inventory tracking and service-history indexing should reduce search time and missing evidence, not automate technical judgments. End every review with cash remaining, inventory age, open obligations, and the next dated decision. Scale the repeatable control system before scaling the stock.
